artiest/alexander-glazunov.text:
Alexander Glazunov was a Russian composer, teacher and conductor of the late Romantic era. He was born in St Petersburg in 1865, the son of a wealthy publisher. He began piano lessons at nine and started composing at eleven. Mily Balakirev brought his work to the attention of Rimsky-Korsakov, who gave him private lessons. In 1882 Rimsky-Korsakov conducted his first orchestral work, when Glazunov was sixteen. Borodin and Vladimir Stasov praised him lavishly. Later, the timber merchant Mitrofan Belyayev helped him with publications and concerts.

Glazunov wrote eight completed symphonies. His most popular works are the ballets The Seasons and Raymonda, a few of the later symphonies and his Violin Concerto, a favourite of Jascha Heifetz. He gained international recognition and in 1889 conducted his Second Symphony in Paris. From 1905 to 1928 he directed the St Petersburg Conservatory. The best-known student of that period was Dmitri Shostakovich. In 1928 he travelled to Europe and the United States, and he settled in Paris, where he died in 1936.

Glazunov brought together nationalism and international style. He followed Balakirev but stood closer to the epic grandeur of Borodin, and he took on the orchestral colour of Rimsky-Korsakov and the melody of Tchaikovsky. Younger composers such as Prokofiev and Shostakovich found his work old-fashioned, but he remained a steadying presence in a turbulent age.
artiest/alexander-glazunov.listen: Listen to a piece from the ballet The Seasons and notice how the orchestra paints the different seasons in rich tone colours.

artiest/alexander-scriabin.text:
Alexander Scriabin was a Russian composer and pianist, born in Moscow in 1872 into a noble family. His mother, a concert pianist, died when he was one year old. He studied at the Moscow Conservatory with Anton Arensky and Sergei Taneyev, among others. He became a respected pianist, despite his small hands, which could barely span a ninth. In 1894 he made his debut in St Petersburg with his own music. That same year he signed a contract with the publisher Mitrofan Belyayev.

His early music follows Frédéric Chopin and sounds late Romantic. He then developed, independently of Arnold Schoenberg, a highly dissonant musical language that left traditional tonality behind without being strictly atonal. It came with a philosophy of its own, with the idea of the Gesamtkunstwerk and synaesthesia. Inspired by theosophy, he devised a colour wheel based on the circle of fifths that linked sounds to colours. His works include ten published piano sonatas, the Poem of Ecstasy and the Third Symphony, which was performed in Paris in 1905. In 1904 he moved to Geneva.

Scriabin was one of the most controversial composer-pianists of the early twentieth century. Tolstoy called his music the sincere expression of a genius. He was regarded as the most important Russian Symbolist composer and inspired Karol Szymanowski, among others. Since the 1970s his music has been rediscovered more and more. He died in 1915.
artiest/alexander-scriabin.listen: Listen to an early piano piece by Scriabin and compare it with a late sonata: notice how the sound of Chopin slowly turns into something unpredictable and dissonant.

artiest/alexander-von-schlippenbach.text:
Alexander von Schlippenbach is a German jazz pianist and composer, born in 1938. He began piano lessons at the age of eight and studied composition in Cologne with Bernd Alois Zimmermann. While still a student he was already playing with Manfred Schoof. At twenty-eight he founded the Globe Unity Orchestra, a large ensemble for free jazz. In the 1960s he became known as the pianist in a trio with saxophonist Evan Parker and drummer Paul Lovens.

In 1988 he founded the Berlin Contemporary Jazz Orchestra, a big band in which Willem Breuker, Misha Mengelberg, Evan Parker, Kenny Wheeler and his wife Aki Takase, among others, played. He played extensively within the European free jazz community and worked for German radio stations. In 1994 he received the Albert Mangelsdorff Prize. His albums include Globe Unity from 1967, The Living Music from 1972 and Smoke from 1990.

From the 1980s onwards he also immersed himself in older jazz composers, such as Jelly Roll Morton and Thelonious Monk. In 2005 he recorded the complete works of Monk, released as Monk's Casino. In doing so he showed that free jazz and tradition are not far apart, and that a pianist from the avant-garde can listen to a classic with the same curiosity.
artiest/alexander-von-schlippenbach.listen: Listen to Monk's Casino and notice how he keeps Monk's familiar melodies recognisable while playing them with unexpected accents and silences.

artiest/alexander-zemlinsky.text:
Alexander Zemlinsky was an Austrian composer, conductor and teacher, born in Vienna in 1871 into a family of mixed origins. He studied piano and entered the Vienna Conservatory in 1884. There he was taught by Anton Bruckner, among others. Johannes Brahms supported him, attended a performance of his work in 1892 and recommended his Klarinettrio to a publisher. In 1895 Zemlinsky founded the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia. There he met Arnold Schoenberg, who later became his brother-in-law. He taught Schoenberg counterpoint, the only formal music lessons Schoenberg ever received.

Gustav Mahler conducted the premiere of his opera Es war einmal in 1900. Zemlinsky was a conductor in Vienna, in Prague from 1911 to 1927, and then in Berlin. In Prague he conducted the premiere of Schoenberg's Erwartung in 1924. His best-known work is the Lyrische Symphonie of 1923, for soprano, baritone and orchestra, on poems by Tagore. He also wrote the symphonic work Die Seejungfrau, after Hans Christian Andersen. With the rise of the Nazis he fled to Vienna in 1933, and in 1938 to New York via Prague.

In the United States he was barely noticed, while Schoenberg was celebrated in Los Angeles. He died in 1942. His music begins with Brahms and takes in the expanded harmonies of Wagner and Mahler. He became an important link between late Romanticism and the Second Viennese School, and taught Erich Wolfgang Korngold, among others.
artiest/alexander-zemlinsky.listen: Listen to a movement from the Lyrische Symphonie and notice how soprano and baritone alternate above a rich, almost cinematic orchestra.

artiest/alexandre-desplat.text: Alexandre Desplat was born in Paris in 1961 and plays the flute himself. In France he long worked with the director Jacques Audiard, on films including Un héros très discret (1996) and Sur mes lèvres (2001). His international breakthrough was Girl with a Pearl Earring (2003). Desplat writes precisely and transparently, with plenty of woodwinds, harp, piano and small percussion patterns. He often lets rhythm and tone colour matter more than a big theme. For Wes Anderson he used cimbalom, balalaikas and organ in The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014). That score won an Oscar, as did The Shape of Water (2017) by Guillermo del Toro.
artiest/alexandre-desplat.listen: Notice the clear, rhythmic patterns in flute, harp and piano, and the unusual folk instruments in The Grand Budapest Hotel.

artiest/alexandre-tharaud.text:
Alexandre Tharaud is a French pianist, born in Paris in 1968. His mother was a dance teacher at the Opéra de Paris and his father sang and directed operettas as an amateur. He began piano lessons at the age of five. At fourteen he entered the Paris Conservatoire, and at seventeen he won first prize for piano there. In 1987 he won third prize at the Barcelona competition and in 1989 second prize at the ARD competition in Munich. His career developed quickly in Europe, North America and Japan.

He recorded a large, varied discography. It includes Rameau, Scarlatti, Debussy and Poulenc, as well as Le Bœuf sur le toit : Swinging Paris from 2012. He worked with the actor François Morel on a show about Erik Satie and organised a Satie day with the singer Juliette. In 2012 he played himself in Michael Haneke's film Amour. In 2005 The New York Times described his Bach as sharply articulated and vividly drawn. In 2015 he was the central soloist at the Prinsengrachtconcert in Amsterdam.

Tharaud has no piano at home, because he fears he would then rather improvise than work hard. He practises at friends' homes on a variety of instruments. Before every recording he lays flowers on the grave of Emmanuel Chabrier. He has written two books about his life as a musician. In this way he shows that a classical pianist can find a voice of his own in cabaret, film and books too.
artiest/alexandre-tharaud.listen: Listen to Le Bœuf sur le toit : Swinging Paris and notice how he brings the light, Parisian atmosphere of the 1920s to life on the piano.

artiest/alfred-brendel.text:
Alfred Brendel was an Austrian pianist, poet and writer, born in Czechoslovakia in 1931 and based in London. He grew up in Zagreb and Graz, where his father was, among other things, a hotel manager and a cinema manager. He had piano lessons from the age of six and after the age of sixteen was largely self-taught. At seventeen he gave his first public recital in Graz, with a programme on the fugue in piano music. In 1949 he won fourth prize at the Busoni Competition in Bolzano.

He made his first recording in 1950, of Prokofiev's Fifth Piano Concerto. In 1952 he was the first to record Liszt's Weihnachtsbaum. He made three complete recordings of Beethoven's 32 piano sonatas and was the first to record all of Beethoven's solo works. His international breakthrough came after a Beethoven recital at the Queen Elizabeth Hall in London, after which three record companies phoned his manager. In 1971 he moved to Hampstead. For Philips he recorded Mozart's piano concertos with Neville Marriner and the Academy of St Martin in the Fields. He also played a great deal of Liszt, Brahms, Schumann and above all Schubert.

Brendel gave concerts in Europe, the United States, South America, Japan and Australia, and had a close bond with the Vienna and Berlin Philharmonic Orchestras. He died in 2025. He showed that a pianist who thinks, writes and paints can also play the great classical works with fresh attention, and his recordings remain a benchmark for Beethoven and Schubert.
artiest/alfred-brendel.listen: Listen to the Diabelli Variations (1972) and notice how he gives each variation its own character, from humour to gravity.

artiest/alfred-drake.text:
Alfred Drake was an American actor and singer, born Alfred Capurro in New York in 1914 to parents from Recco, near Genoa. He began his Broadway career while a student at Brooklyn College. He was primarily a stage and television actor and made only one film, Tars and Spars in 1946. He did play small roles on television and was heard as a voice in a Rankin-Bass film about Santa Claus. He also had a part in Trading Places in 1983.

His best-known work was done on the stage. He played the leading roles in the original Broadway productions of Oklahoma! and Kiss Me, Kate, and sang the title song in Babes in Arms. For his role as Hajj in Kismet he received a Tony Award. Kismet, from 1953, used the music of Alexander Borodin for songs such as Stranger in Paradise. He also played a great deal of Shakespeare, including Benedick in Much Ado About Nothing opposite Katharine Hepburn, and in 1964 Claudius in the Hamlet with Richard Burton. His last Broadway musical was Gigi in 1973 and 1974.

Drake also directed and wrote plays, and a book about gin rummy. From 1970 to 1978 he was president of The Players, a theatre club in New York. In 1981 he was inducted into the American Theatre Hall of Fame. He died in 1992. He shows how a singer on a Broadway stage uses his voice as an actor, with clear diction and a strong theatrical sense.
artiest/alfred-drake.listen: Listen to the album Kismet and notice how the singing voice delivers the narrative lyrics with clarity against the backdrop of the lyrical music.

artiest/alfred-newman.text: Alfred Newman was born in New Haven in 1900, the eldest of ten children, and played the piano in theatres from an early age. He conducted on Broadway and came to Hollywood in 1930. His melody for Street Scene (1931), a jazzy portrait of the city, was later used again and again. He wrote the famous 20th Century Fox fanfare and from 1940 headed that studio's music department. Together with sound engineers he developed a warm, glossy string sound, the Newman sound. Newman won nine Oscars, more than any other film composer. His works include Wuthering Heights (1939), The Song of Bernadette (1943) and The Robe (1953). His sons Thomas and David and his nephew Randy also became film composers.
artiest/alfred-newman.listen: Notice the sound of the strings: plenty of vibrato, long singing lines and a warm, glossy blend.

artiest/alfredo-marceneiro.text:
Alfredo Rodrigo Duarte was born in Lisbon in 1891 and died there in 1982. His stage name Marceneiro comes from his original trade: the Portuguese word means cabinetmaker. He sang fado, the Portuguese music of longing and fate, and is still regarded as a yardstick for generations of fado singers.

Marceneiro wrote the music of his songs himself. The lyrics mostly came from others, such as Silva Tavares and Henrique Rêgo. His best-known songs include A Casa da Mariquinhas, Sinas, Rainha Santa and Moinho Desmantelado. The music is usually simple, in a calm 2/4 time, played on string instruments, the Portuguese guitar and the ordinary guitar.

His way of singing was distinctive. His voice was on the verge of breaking. He sang calmly, almost in the manner of a storyteller, and rarely let rip. He usually stood with both hands in his trouser pockets. It was precisely this restrained manner that made an impression: the feeling lies in the voice itself, not in the gesture. After his death he was posthumously awarded a Portuguese honour in 1984, the Order of Infante D. Henrique.
artiest/alfredo-marceneiro.listen: Listen to Há Festa na Mouraria and notice the guitar accompaniment and the restrained, storytelling voice. Try to hear how little the singer forces his voice.

artiest/algebra-blessett.text:
Algebra Blessett is an American R&B singer, born in Atlanta in 1976 and known simply as Algebra. Her mother was a gospel singer and bass player. She grew up with soul, gospel and R&B and sang in the school choir as a girl, mainly so that she could stay on after school with her friends. She started out as a backing singer, for Monica and Bilal among others, and through this obtained a contract with Rowdy Records in Atlanta.

She toured with Anthony Hamilton and worked with India.Arie. Later she learned to play the guitar and played in clubs in Atlanta herself. She writes her own songs. Her first single, U Do It For Me, was released in 2006 on Kedar Entertainment. Her first album, Purpose, followed in 2008 and spent fourteen weeks on the Billboard R&B chart. Her second album, Recovery from 2014, reached the Billboard 200.

Her music is regarded as R&B or neo-soul, with influences from jazz, gospel and rock. In this way she fits into a movement of female singers who carry soul forward in a personal way.
artiest/algebra-blessett.listen: Listen to Recovery and notice how her voice moves between soft soul and gospel-like power.

artiest/alhaji-k-frimpong.text:
Alhaji Mohammed Ibrahim Kwame Frimpong was born in 1939 in Ofoase in the Ashanti region, in what was then the Gold Coast and later became Ghana. Under the name K. Frimpong he became a singer of highlife, the popular dance music of Ghana. His best-known song is Kyenkyen Bi Adi M'awu, released under the name K. Frimpong And His Cubano Fiestas.

In the 1970s he recorded with two different bands whose line-ups partly overlapped. One of these was the Vis-A-Vis band from Kumasi, led by Isaac Yeboah. Their album Obi Agye Me Dofo was released in Ghana on the Probisco label and was later reissued by Makossa International. Frimpong's later albums include Abrabo from 1984 and K. Frimpong Backed by Vis-A-Vis, which appeared in 2020.

Highlife is a style of music in which African rhythms and guitar parts are combined with brass instruments and other influences from elsewhere. Frimpong used that form for songs in Twi, the language of the Ashanti. He died in Kumasi in 2005. His two sons are rappers under the names Cabum and Kofi Kapone, which shows how the music of Ghana took on a new form in the next generation.
artiest/alhaji-k-frimpong.listen: Listen to Kyenkyen Bi Adi M'awu and notice the interplay of the guitars and the rhythm section. Try to hear how the voice and the accompaniment take turns.

artiest/ali-akbar-khan.text:
Ali Akbar Khan was born in 1922 in Shibpur, in present-day Bangladesh, the son of the musician and teacher Allauddin Khan. The family moved to Maihar in present-day Madhya Pradesh, where his father was court musician. He learned vocal music and several instruments, but ultimately chose the sarod. Lessons began before sunrise and sometimes lasted eighteen hours a day. In 1936, at the age of thirteen, he made his debut at a music conference in Allahabad, and in 1939 he accompanied Ravi Shankar there, the first of many duets between the two.

In 1955, at the invitation of Yehudi Menuhin, he travelled to the United States, where he recorded Music of India: Morning and Evening Ragas in New York. He also composed new ragas, such as Chandranandan, and film music, including for Satyajit Ray's Devi. In 1956 he founded the Ali Akbar College of Music in Calcutta, and in 1967 a second one in Berkeley, later based in San Rafael. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 1989 and a MacArthur Fellowship in 1991. He also taught Mickey Hart of the Grateful Dead to play.

His style was restrained and deeply expressive. He drew great intensity and tone colour from a few notes and simple melodic lines, rather than outward show. In this way he brought Hindustani classical music to the West and became one of the most highly regarded Indian musicians of the twentieth century. He died in San Anselmo in 2009.
artiest/ali-akbar-khan.listen: Listen to Sindhi Bhairavi and notice how the sarod builds an atmosphere with a slow beginning. Follow how the melody gradually speeds up and how the tabla joins in later.

artiest/ali-farka-toure.text: Ali Farka Touré grew up in Niafunké on the River Niger. Because his noble caste was not allowed to make music, as a boy he secretly built a one-stringed instrument, and later he learned the guitar. His hypnotic guitar patterns reminded Western listeners of John Lee Hooker, although he insisted that it was not blues. With Ry Cooder he made Talking Timbuktu (1994), which won a Grammy.
artiest/ali-farka-toure.listen: Listen to Diaraby and hear how the guitar keeps repeating the same short pattern, with small variations, as in early blues.

artiest/ali-shaheed-muhammad.text:
Ali Shaheed Muhammad is an American DJ, producer, rapper and bass guitarist, born in Brooklyn in 1970 and raised in Bedford-Stuyvesant. He began DJing at the age of eight and programming music at thirteen. At secondary school he became friends with Q-Tip. In 1985 they made demos together, using recording equipment belonging to his uncle. Phife Dawg and Jarobi White then joined them, and so A Tribe Called Quest came into being.

With Q-Tip and Phife Dawg he made five studio albums between 1990 and 1998. With Q-Tip and Jay Dee he founded the production collective the Ummah. After the group split up he formed the R&B supergroup Lucy Pearl with Dawn Robinson and Raphael Saadiq, which made an album in 2000. His solo debut Shaheedullah and Stereotypes followed in 2004. In 2013 he moved to Los Angeles to work with the producer Adrian Younge. Together they made the music for both seasons of the TV series Luke Cage and toured as The Midnight Hour. In 2020 they began the Jazz Is Dead album series, with jazz musicians including Roy Ayers, Marcos Valle, Doug Carn, Gary Bartz and João Donato. He is the principal bass guitarist on it.

From 2013 to 2016 he hosted the NPR radio show Microphone Check. In 2024 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of A Tribe Called Quest. He shows how hip hop and jazz can find each other, from the samples of the 1990s to the live jazz of today.
artiest/ali-shaheed-muhammad.listen: Listen to an album from the Jazz Is Dead series, for instance the one with Roy Ayers, and notice the role of the bass and how the jazz sounds both warm and raw.

artiest/alice-coltrane.text: Alice McLeod grew up in Detroit, played organ in church and in 1959 studied in Paris with Bud Powell. In 1965 she married John Coltrane and replaced McCoy Tyner as the pianist in his group. After Coltrane's death in 1967 she made her own albums for Impulse!, on which she played harp, piano and organ. Journey in Satchidananda (1971), with Pharoah Sanders, shows influences from Indian music, with a tanpura drone and long modal lines. She became a follower of an Indian guru and in 1983 founded an ashram in California, where she recorded devotional music. Her great-nephew is Flying Lotus.
artiest/alice-coltrane.listen: Listen to the harp: gliding waves over a repeated bass line.

artiest/alicia-keys.text:
Alicia Keys, born Alicia Augello Cook, came into the world in 1981 in Hell's Kitchen, a rough neighbourhood of Manhattan. Her mother raised her alone and played jazz records by Billie Holiday, Ella Fitzgerald and Thelonious Monk on Sunday mornings. From the age of seven Keys had classical piano lessons and played Beethoven, Mozart and Chopin. At twelve she wrote her first song and at fifteen she signed with Columbia Records.

After a dispute with that label she released her debut Songs in A Minor on J Records in 2001. The album won five Grammys and contained the number one hit Fallin'. Next came The Diary of Alicia Keys (2003) with If I Ain't Got You, As I Am (2007) with No One, and The Element of Freedom (2009). That same year she sang the chorus of Jay-Z's Empire State of Mind. With Girl on Fire (2012) she again reached the top of the American album chart. Later she wrote the Broadway musical Hell's Kitchen, about the neighbourhood where she grew up.

Keys combines classical piano with soul, R&B and hip hop. The piano is often central for her, with a warm, powerful voice above it. This made her one of the most important R&B artists of the 2000s. Her music also shows how hip hop changed pop production: drum patterns from old records gained a new life in modern hits.
artiest/alicia-keys.listen: Listen to Girl on Fire. Notice the heavy, resonant drum beats: that pattern comes from The Big Beat by Billy Squier from 1980. Hear how the old rock rhythm carries a new soul song beneath the piano and Keys's voice.

artiest/alim-qasimov.text:
Alim Qasimov is an Azerbaijani singer and one of the most important singers of mugham, the classical vocal repertoire of Azerbaijan. He was born in 1957 in the village of Nabur near Shamakhi, about a hundred kilometres north of Baku. His family worked on a Soviet collective farm. His father made him a simple drum from a window frame and goat's stomach lining. He began singing at religious gatherings and at twenty-one went to the music school in Baku.

Under Soviet rule mugham received little support. In 1983 he won a national singing competition. He then won prizes at the UNESCO symposia of 1983 and 1987. In the 1990s he toured Iran, Brazil, the United States and Europe, among other places. At a festival in France he met Jeff Buckley, with whom he sang a duet that appears on Buckley's Live à l'Olympia. In 1993 he became People's Artist of Azerbaijan and in 1999 he won the IMC-UNESCO Music Prize. He recorded nine albums, three of them with his daughter Farghana Qasimova, such as Love's Deep Ocean from 2000.

His style is based on improvisation, and he also took over elements from ashiq, a rural singing tradition. The qawwali singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan was a great inspiration to him. The New York Times called him one of the greatest singers alive. In 2012 he sang along at the Eurovision Song Contest in Baku. He made the old form of mugham sound like a living, personal art.
artiest/alim-qasimov.listen: Listen to a long vocal piece by Qasimov, such as on Love's Deep Ocean, and notice how his voice slowly builds from restrained to fiery.

artiest/alim-qasimov-en-malik-mansurov.text:
Alim Qasimov was born in 1957 in the village of Nabur near Shamakhi in Azerbaijan, some hundred kilometres north of Baku. His family worked on a Soviet collective farm and he helped out from an early age. He began singing at religious gatherings. At fourteen, during a local competition, he was laughed off the stage by the audience, who thought he had not mastered the traditional style. He persevered and became one of the most important singers of mugham, the classical music of Azerbaijan.

In Soviet times mugham received no support from the state and was seen by the party mainly as a local curiosity. Even so, Qasimov gained international recognition, including at UNESCO symposia in 1983 and 1987. He combined mugham with ashiq, a bardic tradition of the countryside, and was influenced by the qawwali singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan. In the 1990s he toured Iran, Brazil, the United States and Europe, among other places, and worked with Jeff Buckley. In 1993 he became People's Artist of Azerbaijan and in 1999 he won the UNESCO Music Prize of the International Music Council. Malik Mansurov performed with him and was mentioned by The New York Times as a highlight of a festival.

Qasimov's voice is best known for its vocal improvisation. The New York Times called him one of the greatest singers in the world. In 2012 he sang along at the Eurovision Song Contest in Baku.
artiest/alim-qasimov-en-malik-mansurov.listen: Listen to Bayati Shiraz and notice how the voice embellishes the melody again and again and lets it grow. Try to hear how the accompaniment stays beneath it and leaves the singer free to move.

artiest/alla-rakha.text:
Alla Rakha was an Indian tabla player in Hindustani classical music, born in 1919 in a village in Jammu. At twelve he ran away from home to learn music. In Gurdaspur he became a pupil of Mian Kader Baksh, who adopted him and designated him as his successor as head of the Punjab tabla school. He also had singing lessons. In 1936 he worked for All India Radio in Lahore, and later in Bombay. From 1943 he composed for almost two dozen Hindi and Punjabi films, until in 1958 he turned to classical music.

His collaboration with Ravi Shankar began in the early 1950s and lasted almost thirty years. Their performances at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967 and at Woodstock in 1969 brought Indian classical music to a large Western audience. He also played at the Concert for Bangladesh in 1971. In 1968 he made the album Rich à la Rakha with the jazz drummer Buddy Rich. Mickey Hart of the Grateful Dead admired him and studied his technique. In 1985 Alla Rakha founded the Alla Rakha Institute of Music in Mumbai.

His son Zakir Hussain also became a tabla player. Alla Rakha made the tabla known and loved in the West, and also bridged the gap between Carnatic and Hindustani music. He died in 2000.
artiest/alla-rakha.listen: Listen to Rich à la Rakha and notice how the tabla converses with a jazz drummer, with a steady rhythm and lightning-fast patterns.

artiest/allauddin-khan.text:
Allauddin Khan was an Indian sarod player, composer and one of the most important music teachers of the twentieth century in Indian classical music. He was probably born around 1881 in the village of Shibpur in East Bengal. His father was an amateur sitar player. Even as a child he responded strongly to music, and he skipped school to attend religious and musical gatherings. At the age of eight he ran away from home to join a group of travelling musicians.

He eventually became court musician in Maihar, after an audition arranged by the maharaja there. There he trained pupils who lived with him. His method was extremely strict: at first, pupils were not allowed to hear any other music or to play in public. Even his own son, Ali Akbar Khan, had to concentrate exclusively on music. In 1918, after the influenza epidemic, he founded the Maihar Band, made up of orphaned children who thus received shelter and work.

At a time when North Indian classical music was mainly vocal and instruments only accompanied, he helped to establish instrumental music as an independent solo form. He broke with the secretive and exclusive habits of his day and trained world-famous virtuosos, from his own family and beyond, who made Indian classical music known abroad as well. He received a Fellowship of the Sangeet Natak Akademi in 1954, the Padma Bhushan in 1958 and the Padma Vibhushan in 1971. He died in 1972.
artiest/allauddin-khan.listen: Listen to a sarod recording by his pupil or son Ali Akbar Khan and notice how the instrument calmly builds a raga before the tempo picks up.

artiest/aloe-blacc.text:
Aloe Blacc is an American singer, songwriter, rapper and producer, born Egbert Nathaniel Dawkins III in 1979 in Orange County, California, to Panamanian parents. He began with a rented trumpet in third grade and at around the same time was gripped by LL Cool J. He studied linguistics and psychology at the University of Southern California and worked briefly at Ernst & Young. In 1995 he formed the hip hop duo Emanon with the producer Exile, named after a Dizzy Gillespie tune.

With breakbeats and jazz samples, Emanon became an established name in underground rap. In 2003 he began a solo career and in 2006 he signed with Stones Throw Records, which released his album Shine Through. His big breakthrough came with Good Things in 2010. It featured I Need a Dollar, which became the theme song of an HBO series. In 2013 he co-wrote Wake Me Up with Avicii and sang on it. The song reached number one in twenty-two countries. Lift Your Spirit, his major-label debut, was released in November 2013. The Man also reached number one in the UK.

His music combines soul with hip hop. He did not want to express ego, as in much hip hop, but to write songs that say more. In this way he fits into the line of singers who combine soul and social awareness.
artiest/aloe-blacc.listen: Listen to I Need a Dollar and notice how his soul voice sounds over a simple accompaniment, and what the lyrics say about money.

artiest/altamiro-carrilho.text:
Altamiro Carrilho was born Altamiro Aquino Carrilho in 1924 and died in Rio de Janeiro in 2012. He was a Brazilian musician and composer, regarded as a master flautist and as one of the most important representatives of choro, the Brazilian folk music of Rio.

Choro is an instrumental style that arose in Rio de Janeiro in the nineteenth century. The flute usually carries the melody, accompanied by guitars and percussion. The style is lively and virtuosic, with fast melodic lines that circle around one another almost playfully. Carrilho released the albums Dobrados em Desfile in 1959, Rio Antigo in 1961, Choros imortais №2 in 1965 and Antologia do Chorinho in 1975, among others. In this way he kept the old repertoire alive and made it known to a large audience.

In the course he stands for the work of Joaquim Callado, whose A Flor Amorosa dates from 1880. Callado was a nineteenth-century flautist and an early figure in choro. That Carrilho played this piece shows that choro is a tradition in which a player takes over the work of his predecessors. His playing is regarded as an example for later flautists.
artiest/altamiro-carrilho.listen: Listen to A Flor Amorosa and notice the flute carrying the melody, with guitars beneath. Try to hear how the flautist lets the line dance lightly.

artiest/alva-noto.text:
Alva Noto is the musical name of Carsten Nicolai, a German artist and label owner, born in 1965 in Karl-Marx-Stadt, now Chemnitz, in the GDR. He studied landscape architecture in Dresden and, as an independent visual artist, exhibited at a time when private galleries did not exist in the GDR. After the fall of the Wall he co-founded the cultural centre VOXXX in Chemnitz. In 1994 he started the label noton, which merged with RasterMusic in 1999 to form Raster-Noton.

Raster-Noton became an important German platform for experimental electronic music. Nicolai was responsible there for the CD series 20 to 2000, which won the Golden Nica at Prix Ars Electronica in 2000. His music as Alva Noto is reductive and connected with his visual work, with signs, acoustics and visual structures. His albums include Prototypes from 2000, Transform from 2001, the Xerrox series and unitxt from 2008. He worked with Ryōji Ikeda, Blixa Bargeld, Michael Nyman and Iggy Pop, and above all with Ryūichi Sakamoto.

In 2009 he wrote the opera Sparkie: Cage and Beyond with Nyman. In 2015 he made the music for Alejandro González Iñárritu's The Revenant together with Sakamoto, which was nominated for a Golden Globe and a BAFTA, among others. He showed how electronic music can sound almost like visual art, and took his work to museums such as Tate Modern and the Centre Pompidou.
artiest/alva-noto.listen: Listen to a piece from the Xerrox series and notice how small electronic sounds and rhythms form a tight, almost bare structure.

artiest/amadeus-quartet.text:
The Amadeus Quartet was a string quartet that existed from 1947 to 1987 without a single change of member in all those years. Three of its members, the violinists Norbert Brainin and Siegmund Nissel and the later violist Peter Schidlof, had to flee Vienna as young Jews after the Anschluss in 1938. They met in British internment camps and afterwards studied free of charge with Max Rostal. Through him they came into contact with the cellist Martin Lovett. In 1947 they formed the Brainin Quartet, which became the Amadeus Quartet in 1948.

The first concert under that name was on 10 January 1948 at the Wigmore Hall in London. The quartet made about two hundred recordings, including all the quartets of Beethoven, Brahms and Mozart. For string quintets and sextets it invited Cecil Aronowitz and William Pleeth. Albums such as String Quintets K 516 & K 593 from 1961 and Der Tod und das Mädchen from 1982 belong to this body of work. Benjamin Britten wrote his last string quartet for them. They played it for the first time after his death.

The quartet was known for its smooth, refined style, seamless ensemble playing and sensitive interpretation, and was often regarded as Austrian, although it was formed and based in the United Kingdom. It ceased to exist in 1987 when Peter Schidlof died. For many listeners the recordings have become the yardstick for Mozart and Beethoven.
artiest/amadeus-quartet.listen: Listen to Der Tod und das Mädchen and notice how the four strings play together as a whole and yet each keeps its own voice.

artiest/amalia-rodrigues.text: Amália Rodrigues sold fruit in the port of Lisbon as a girl and sang fado professionally for the first time in 1939. Through films and performances, including at the Olympia in Paris, she brought fado to the whole world. From the 1960s she worked with the composer Alain Oulman, who set poems to music. In 2001 she became the first woman to be interred in Portugal's National Pantheon.
artiest/amalia-rodrigues.listen: Listen to Barco Negro: the Portuguese guitar, with its clear, shimmering sound, plays between the phrases, and Amália's voice deliberately breaks on the high notes.

artiest/american-quartet.text:
The American Quartet was a vocal quartet that recorded for various companies in the United States between 1899 and 1925. The line-up changed over the years. The name was first used around 1899 for the group that later became better known as the Haydn Quartet, with John Bieling, Jere Mahoney, S. H. Dudley and William F. Hooley.

The best-known line-up arose in 1909, when Victor Records was looking for an ensemble for its new star, the tenor Billy Murray. Around him were Bieling and Hooley, who also continued to sing in the Haydn Quartet, and Steve Porter, who came from the Peerless Quartet. In 1910 they recorded Casey Jones, perhaps the first record in American music history to sell a million copies. Bieling left the group in 1913 because his voice suffered from the yodelling and cowboy yells that some records demanded. Robert Armour took his place and John Young later followed. Hooley died of Spanish flu in 1918 and Donald Chalmers became the bass. Later Murray sang with a new group, with Albert Campbell, John Meyer and Frank Croxton, under the same name for Victor.

The American Quartet shows what popular music sounded like early in the twentieth century, before radio and electrical recording: four male voices in tight harmony, with a piano or small orchestra behind them and a clear diction that could be understood even through the acoustic horn. Their songs, including some about the First World War, formed the foundation of the record industry.
artiest/american-quartet.listen: Listen to It's a Long Way to Tipperary and notice how four voices together carry the melody and how clearly the words can be understood. Can you hear the emphasis on the chorus?

artiest/ami-faku.text:
Amanda Faku, known as Ami Faku, was born in 1993 in the township of eZinyoka near Port Elizabeth in South Africa. By the age of six she already loved music and sang in church choirs, including in the home church where her father was pastor. She cites influences from church, reggae and hip hop. In 2012 she began recording, with a producer who lived a few streets from her home.

Her breakthrough came in 2017 as a contestant on the second season of The Voice SA. She did not win, but she did sign a contract with the label The Vth Season. Her first single was Ndikhethe Wena. She then worked with De Mogul SA on Ungowam, and in 2020 uWrongo by DJ Prince Kaybee, with Shimza and Black Motion, was released. The collaboration with Sun-El Musician on Into Ingawe followed. In 2019 her debut album Imali came out, which debuted at number one in South Africa. It was certified gold by RiSA. In 2020 the newspaper Mail & Guardian put her on its list of two hundred young South Africans.

Her music lies close to the South African house scene, with a warm, soulful voice over electronic rhythms. She sings mainly in Xhosa. She shows how a singer from the township can reach a large audience through a television competition.
artiest/ami-faku.listen: Listen to Asibe Happy and notice the warm voice and how, together with the rhythms, it creates a calm, cheerful atmosphere. Also notice the language she sings in.

artiest/amina-claudine-myers.text: Pianist, organist and singer Amina Claudine Myers grew up in Arkansas and Texas and sang gospel in church as a child. In the 1960s she came to Chicago, where she became a member of the AACM. She played with Lester Bowie, Muhal Richard Abrams, Henry Threadgill and Arthur Blythe. Her music combines gospel and blues with the freedom of the avant-garde. On Amina Claudine Myers Salutes Bessie Smith (1980) she honours one of the first blues singers. She also wrote works for choir and theatre.
artiest/amina-claudine-myers.listen: Hear the gospel in the organ and the blues in the voice.

artiest/amir-khusrau.text: Amir Khusrau was a poet and musician in Delhi and a disciple of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya, beside whom he is buried. He lived from about 1253 to 1325. Tradition calls him the father of qawwali, the sung Sufi prayer, although many of the musical inventions attributed to him cannot be proven. Songs bearing his name, such as Chhap Tilak, are still sung at the shrines of saints across South Asia.
artiest/amir-khusrau.listen: Of course, no recordings of Khusrau himself exist. Listen to Abida Parveen in Chaap Tilak, a text attributed to him, and hear how a single line returns with ever greater intensity.

artiest/amjad-ali-khan.text:
Amjad Ali Khan is an Indian sarod player, born on 9 October 1945 as Masoom Ali Khan. He comes from a classical music family, the Bangash line of the Senia Gharana, and is the sixth generation of musicians in his lineage. His family claims to have invented the sarod. His father Hafiz Ali Khan, court musician in Gwalior, was his first teacher. In 1957 the family moved to Delhi.

Khan first performed in the United States in 1963 and was afterwards in demand on stages all over the world, often together with his sons Amaan and Ayaan. Records such as Raga Darbari from 1975, Afternoon Ragas from 1990 and Evening Raga from 2001 show how broad his repertoire is. He played with Western orchestras and taught at universities. He also composed new ragas, such as Haripriya Kanada, Shyam Shri and Priyadarshini. He himself does not call them a new creation, but a continuation of the tradition.

The sarod is a fretless string instrument with a metal fingerboard, on which the player can bend the pitch with a gliding motion. Critics praise Khan's technical mastery and his feeling, and above all his clear, lightning-fast ekhara taans, the rapid runs of notes with which he builds a raga. India honoured him with the Padma Shri in 1975, the Padma Bhushan in 1991 and the Padma Vibhushan in 2001. For anyone who encounters Indian classical music as a source of influence in the course, he is one of the most important living voices.
artiest/amjad-ali-khan.listen: Listen to a raga by Amjad Ali Khan and notice how he begins: first slowly and freely, without a fixed pulse, and then faster and faster. Try to hear where the rapid runs of notes take over from the slow build-up of the raga.

artiest/amm.text:
AMM was a British free improvisation group, founded in London in 1965. The first line-up consisted of Keith Rowe on guitar, Lou Gare on saxophone and Eddie Prévost on drums. Rowe and Gare came from Mike Westbrook's jazz band, and Prévost and Gare also played together in a hard bop quintet. It began as an experimental weekend workshop at the Royal College of Art. In 1966 the composer Cornelius Cardew joined on piano and cello, and that year the first record, AMMusic, appeared on Elektra Records UK.

No performance was ever planned. The musicians avoided melody, harmony and a fixed rhythm and sought a blend of sound in which you can hardly tell any more which instrument is making which sound. They used special playing techniques and also amplified everyday objects, such as a glass jar or a coffee tin, with contact microphones. The recordings of 12 June 1968 were later released as The Crypt and are regarded as the moment when the long, droning pieces became the group's hallmark. Musicians came and went. Rowe and Prévost stayed longest, and the pianist John Tilbury joined them around 1980. In the 1980s and 1990s the group sounded quieter and more meditative. Prévost released the records on his own label, Matchless Recordings.

AMM never reached a large audience, but had great influence on improvised music and on the later electro-acoustic scene. The group played its last concert at Café Oto in London on 30 July 2022. For a course on pop and rock, AMM shows how far a group could go when it let go of every convention.
artiest/amm.listen: Listen to an excerpt from The Crypt and try not to look for a melody or a beat. Notice the long, swelling sounds and ask yourself whether you can tell which instrument is making which sound.

artiest/amoco-renegades-steel-orchestra.text:
Amoco Renegades is a steel orchestra from Trinidad, led by the arranger Jit Samaroo. A steel orchestra consists of dozens of players on steelpans, instruments made from oil drums on which the player strikes melodies, chords and bass parts with sticks. The steelpan arose in Trinidad in the twentieth century and belongs to the island's calypso and carnival.

The orchestra came to the attention of a wide public in 1990. On 14 July of that year Jean-Michel Jarre gave a free concert in the Paris business district of La Défense, for an audience of some 2.5 million people. Amoco Renegades played there on steel drums under the direction of Jit Samaroo. The concert coincided with the record Waiting for Cousteau, on which Jarre worked the steelpan and calypso rhythms into his electronic music, and the orchestra played on Calypso.

The collaboration shows how an instrument from Caribbean folk music ended up in an electronic pop production. Jarre's synthesizers gained a warm, rhythmic and acoustic sound as a result.
artiest/amoco-renegades-steel-orchestra.listen: Listen to Calypso by Jean-Michel Jarre and notice the difference between the synthesizers and the metallic, bright sound of the steelpans. Try to hear how the pans carry the rhythm.

artiest/amsterdam-andalusian-orchestra.text:
The Amsterdam Andalusian Orchestra, in Dutch the Amsterdams Andalusisch Orkest, is a Dutch orchestra that focuses on Arab-Andalusian music. It was founded in 2011 by a group of friends in Amsterdam: Mohamed Chairi, Yassine Boussaid, Dwight Breinburg and Mohamed Aadroun. Aadroun, a business manager born in Amsterdam to Moroccan parents, became fascinated by the musical heritage of Al-Andalus, medieval Islamic Spain. The orchestra aims to connect that tradition, which is still alive in the countries of the Maghreb, with the cultural life of the Netherlands.

The repertoire stretches from Granada to Baghdad. There is room for classical Arabic music, mystical music from the Middle East, jazz and flamenco. The orchestra likes to work with other art forms, such as poetry, dance and photography. In 2021 it presented the programme The Tree of Being at the Bimhuis, to poems by Ibn Arabi. It has played with Estrella Morente, Sami Yusuf, Cappella Amsterdam, the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra and the Metropole Orkest, and has performed at the Holland Festival and Le Guess Who?, among others. The album Mystic Mirrors was released in 2020.

Together with the theatre De Meervaart, the orchestra organises the biennial Ud Festival, and in 2021, with De Meervaart and the photography museum FOAM, it founded the cultural centre Maqam in Amsterdam-West. In 2024 it received the Cultuurfonds Prijs. It shows how ancient music from the Mediterranean can find an audience of its own in a Dutch city.
artiest/amsterdam-andalusian-orchestra.listen: Listen to a piece from Mystic Mirrors and notice the melody of the voice or the oud, the Arabic lute. Try to hear how the rhythm of the percussion carries the melody.

artiest/amy-winehouse.text:
Amy Winehouse (14 September 1983 to 23 July 2011) was a British singer and songwriter from Enfield, London. She grew up in a household where a lot of jazz was played. Several uncles were professional jazz musicians, and her father sang Frank Sinatra and Tony Bennett at home. She sang in the National Youth Jazz Orchestra, signed with Island Records in 2002 and made her debut Frank, with the producer Salaam Remi, in 2003. She co-wrote almost all the songs herself. The record was full of jazz influences, and her voice was compared with that of Sarah Vaughan.

With Back to Black in 2006 came her worldwide breakthrough. She now drew inspiration from the girl groups and the soul of the 1950s and 1960s. For this she took the Dap-Kings, Sharon Jones's band, into the studio, alongside Salaam Remi and the producer Mark Ronson. The single Rehab became a worldwide hit. In 2008 she won five Grammys, including Record of the Year and Song of the Year. Her dark contralto and her autobiographical lyrics together formed a sound of her own.

Winehouse had serious problems with addiction and her health, and died of alcohol poisoning. Her life was revisited in the documentary Amy in 2015 and the film Back to Black in 2024. She gave the retro soul sound of the 1950s and 1960s new life in the pop music of the twenty-first century and in doing so set off a wave of soul singers.
artiest/amy-winehouse.listen: Listen to Rehab and notice the interplay between her voice, the horns and the rhythm section. Can you hear how the production deliberately sounds like a soul record from the 1960s?

artiest/and-the-mysterians.text:
? and the Mysterians, also Question Mark and the Mysterians, is an American garage rock band from Bay City and Saginaw in Michigan. They were active from 1962 to 1969, with reunions later. The band members were children of Mexican seasonal labourers who had settled in Michigan. The first trio, with Larry Borjas, Robert Martinez and Bobby Balderrama, was inspired by surf bands and guitarists such as Link Wray and Duane Eddy. The singer called himself the question mark and performed with an enigmatic image, borrowed from a 1957 Japanese science fiction film.

In 1966 the group signed with Pa-Go-Go Records in San Antonio. Their first and most acclaimed single was 96 Tears, released in the spring. The original A-side was Midnight Hour, but the question mark had radio stations play the other song. The station CKLW in Windsor, Ontario, in particular played it a lot. It became a number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and kept the band in the spotlight for fifteen months. The following singles, I Need Somebody and Can't Get Enough of You Baby, also reached the charts, but nowhere near as high. The album Action from 1967 showed the band at its best, but sold poorly.

The music revolves around an electronic organ with a sharp, almost ghostly sound, over a simple, hammering accompaniment. 96 Tears is often cited as a precursor of punk. In 2004 it stood at number 210 in Rolling Stone's list of the five hundred greatest songs.
artiest/and-the-mysterians.listen: Listen to 96 Tears and notice the organ that carries the whole song. Hear how the organ riff keeps returning while the singer sounds almost indifferent.

artiest/andre-3000.text:
André 3000 is actually called André Lauren Benjamin. He was born in Atlanta in 1975, where his mother raised him alone. In 1992, at sixteen, he met Antwan Patton, better known as Big Boi, in a shopping mall. Together they formed OutKast. The duo signed with the Atlanta label LaFace and made their debut in 1994 with Southernplayalisticadillacmuzik.

On ATLiens (1996) and Aquemini (1998) OutKast sought new paths, with funk, soul, trip hop and a spacious, relaxed sound. André stood out with surrealist lyrics and an eccentric style, far removed from the gangsta image in hip hop. On Stankonia (2000) he called himself André 3000 for the first time; the single Ms. Jackson became a number one hit. In 2003 came the double album Speakerboxxx/The Love Below, on which each member made a half of his own. André's half was built around funk, jazz and alternative pop, and he sang more than he rapped. His Hey Ya! became a worldwide hit and the album won the Grammy for Album of the Year.

After OutKast he worked mainly as a guest rapper for others and as an actor; he played Jimi Hendrix in a feature film, for instance. In 2023 he surprised everyone with New Blue Sun, an instrumental album on which he plays flute. André 3000 showed that hip hop from the American South could be just as innovative as that of New York or Los Angeles, and that a rapper can also sing and experiment.
artiest/andre-3000.listen: Listen to Hey Ya! by OutKast. Notice the acoustic guitar that opens the song and the handclaps and shouts. Hear how André 3000 mostly sings here rather than raps, as in a cheerful pop song from the 1960s.

artiest/andre-hazes.text:
André Hazes was born in 1951 in the Amsterdam district of De Pijp. At the age of eight he was discovered at the Albert Cuyp market by Johnny Kraaykamp and sang on television. He then did all sorts of jobs, from sailor to butcher's apprentice, before becoming known in his neighbourhood as the singing barman at the café De Krommert. In 1976 Eenzame Kerst was released. In 1977 came the album Zo is het leven, which included De Vlieger, later a Dutch standard.

In 1980 he signed with EMI and his career took off. With Een Vriend and Een Beetje Verliefd, produced by his friend Tim Griek, he reached the top ten in 1981. For the album Gewoon André he received the Zilveren Harp. Hits followed such as Ik Meen 't in 1985, Wij Houden van Oranje in 1988 and Bloed, Zweet en Tranen in 2002. Zij Gelooft in Mij came out in 1981, was recorded again in 1999 and was re-released after his death in 2004. He recorded thirty-six studio and live records.

Hazes sang levenslied: simple, sentimental songs about love, sorrow and life in the city, with a raw, passionate voice. This became hugely popular in the Netherlands and Flanders. He brought the levenslied back to the general public and showed that a folk singer from De Pijp could conquer the charts. He died on 23 September 2004.
artiest/andre-hazes.listen: Listen to Zij gelooft in mij and notice how the voice sounds restrained at the start and then grows stronger. Can you hear the emphasis with which the chorus is sung?

artiest/andrea-gabrieli.text:
Andrea Gabrieli was an Italian composer and organist of the late Renaissance. He was probably born in Venice around 1532 or 1533 and died there on 30 August 1585. Little is known about his youth. He may have studied with Adrian Willaert at San Marco. In 1562 he travelled to Germany, to Frankfurt and Munich, where he became friends with Orlande de Lassus. That friendship strongly shaped his style. In 1566 he became organist of San Marco, one of the most famous musical posts in northern Italy, and he held that position until his death.

Gabrieli wrote a great deal of music for ceremonial occasions, for example for the celebration of the victory at Lepanto in 1571 and for the visit of Japanese princes in 1585. He also composed the choruses for Sophocles' Oedipus tyrannus, for the opening of the Teatro Olimpico in Vicenza. His work includes more than a hundred motets and madrigals, plus a smaller number of instrumental pieces. In San Marco he had groups of singers and instrumentalists answer one another in the enormous, resonant space. In doing so he broke with the strict polyphonic style that dominated the sixteenth century.

Gabrieli published little himself. His nephew Giovanni published much of his music after his death. As a teacher he had famous pupils, including Giovanni Gabrieli and Hans Leo Hassler, who brought the Venetian style to Germany. In this way he became the first internationally known composer of the Venetian school.
artiest/andrea-gabrieli.listen: Listen to a choral piece or a piece for brass by Andrea Gabrieli and notice how the sound is divided. Can you hear how different groups pass the melody to one another, as if they were standing in different places in the church?

artiest/andrea-marcon.text:
Andrea Marcon is an Italian conductor, organist and harpsichordist, born on 6 February 1963 in Treviso. He studied organ and harpsichord with Vanni Ussardi and in 1983 went to the Schola Cantorum Basiliensis in Basel. There he worked with Jean-Claude Zehnder, Jesper Christensen and Jordi Savall, among others. In 1987 he obtained his diplomas in early music, organ and harpsichord. He then specialised in Italian Baroque music with Luigi Ferdinando Tagliavini. He won prizes at organ competitions in Innsbruck in 1986 and Bologna in 1991.

Marcon became a lecturer at the Schola Cantorum in Basel and a visiting professor at the Sweelinck Conservatory in Amsterdam. He founded several ensembles and festivals, such as Sonatori de la Gioiosa Marca in 1983 and, in 1997, the Venice Baroque Orchestra, of which he is the conductor. His early records were organ and harpsichord works, such as Sonate per Organo from 1997. Later came recordings of Baroque opera and concertos, including with Vivaldi and Handel. For these he worked with the violinist Giuliano Carmignola and the singer Magdalena Kožená. He also recorded The Four Seasons in 2000. In 2021 he received the Handel Prize.

Marcon shows how musicians who play early music in a historically informed way, with lively tempos and plenty of rhythmic energy, bring an eighteenth-century repertoire back to life. In this way he contributed to the rediscovery of the Venetian Baroque.
artiest/andrea-marcon.listen: Listen to The Four Seasons in Marcon's performance and notice the colour of the strings and the harpsichord. Can you hear how the orchestra paints the seasons with sharp accents?

artiest/andreas-carlsson.text:
Andreas Carlsson is a Swedish songwriter and music producer, born on 3 April 1973. He was part of the team at Cheiron Studios in Stockholm, the studio where a large share of international teen pop was made in the late 1990s. There, together with Max Martin, he wrote I Want It That Way (1999) for the Backstreet Boys.

When Cheiron closed in 2000, Carlsson and two other former members, Kristian Lundin and Jake Schulze, took over the studio in 2001. Later they started their own production and publishing company. Carlsson often worked with the American songwriter Desmond Child. Among other things he co-wrote Invisible, which Clay Aiken made famous in 2004, and Waking Up in Vegas by Katy Perry. His autobiography appeared in 2009, about the songs that defined his life.

Carlsson's way of working fits the Swedish school of Cheiron: songs in which a catchy melody and a strong chorus matter more than a watertight story. In Sweden he also became known as a judge on Idol and later on X Factor. Nowadays he also gives talks at schools.
artiest/andreas-carlsson.listen: Listen to I Want It That Way by the Backstreet Boys (1999). Notice the chorus: the words sound good but hardly form a logical story, while the melody and the harmonies carry everything.
